questions.stem: A patient treated successfully for breast cancer years ago is now diagnosed with metastases in the hip, spine, liver, and brain. She asks why cancer has appeared in those places when the original cancer was in her breast. What is the best response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cancer in those organs is unrelated to the original breast cancer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Breast cancer cells can spread to distant sites and form metastatic tumors there.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The original breast tumor must have changed into a benign tumor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cancer can spread only to nearby lymph nodes, not distant organs.

questions.rationale: Cancer cells can leave the original tumor, travel to distant sites, and grow there. This spread is called metastasis; the breast remains the primary site and the tumors in distant organs are metastatic or secondary tumors.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why combination chemotherapy uses drugs from different traditional categories?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each drug targets a different step or feature of cancer-cell growth, increasing the chance of killing cancer cells.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each drug prevents every adverse effect caused by the other drugs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drugs are selected only to reduce the number of treatment visits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The combination ensures that only cancer cells are affected.

questions.rationale: Appendix D explains that combination protocols use drugs with different actions to kill more cancer cells. Normal tissues may still be injured, and adverse effects may increase.

questions.stem: Why is chemotherapy given on a planned protocol schedule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A schedule prevents chemotherapy from reaching metastatic sites.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Timing makes chemotherapy affect only cells in the M phase.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The schedule is designed to maximize cancer-cell killing while limiting injury to normal cells.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The schedule eliminates the need to monitor adverse effects.

questions.rationale: The slides describe timed protocols as a way to maximize the number of cancer cells killed and minimize normal-cell damage. Dose-dense schedules may intensify side effects.

questions.stem: Which normal tissues are especially vulnerable to traditional chemotherapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only tissues that contain hormone receptors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tissues whose cells divide rapidly, such as blood-forming tissue, intestinal lining, skin, and hair follicles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only mature nerve and muscle tissue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tissues protected by a distinct capsule.

questions.rationale: Traditional chemotherapy affects cancer cells and normal rapidly dividing cells, including skin, hair, intestinal tissues, and blood-forming cells.

questions.stem: A patient asks why chemotherapy can treat cancer that has spread beyond the original tumor. Which explanation best fits Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Traditional chemotherapy is a local treatment confined to the original tumor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chemotherapy changes metastatic tumors back into benign tumors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chemotherapy works only when cancer cells remain inside a capsule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Traditional chemotherapy is systemic and can reach cancer cells at distant sites.

questions.rationale: Unlike local surgery or radiation, traditional chemotherapy is systemic and may reach metastatic cancer cells, although it also affects normal cells.

questions.stem: Which action is characteristic of an alkylating agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cross-linking DNA strands so they bind together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Imitating normal metabolites in cellular reactions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blocking estrogen production in the adrenal gland.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attaching an antibody to a cancer-cell surface target.

questions.rationale: Appendix D describes alkylating agents as cross-linking DNA strands, interfering with cell division.

questions.stem: How do antimetabolites interfere with cancer-cell growth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They block androgen receptors so testosterone cannot bind.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They form a capsule around the tumor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They resemble normal metabolites and fool cancer cells into using them in cellular reactions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They prevent new blood vessels by blocking an estrogen receptor.

questions.rationale: Antimetabolites resemble normal metabolites needed for vital cell processes and interfere when cancer cells use them.

questions.stem: Which description matches antitumor antibiotics in Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They treat bacterial infections by killing bacteria only.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They bind with DNA and interfere with enzymes needed for DNA replication.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They increase estrogen levels to slow tumor growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They inhibit aldosterone receptors.

questions.rationale: The slides clarify that antitumor antibiotics are not general infection antibiotics; they bind with DNA and block DNA-copying activity.

questions.stem: What is the effect of topoisomerase inhibitors described in Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They increase the sensitivity of insulin receptors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They prevent testosterone from being produced by the testes only.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They make benign tumors invade surrounding tissue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They interfere with an enzyme needed for DNA maintenance, leading to DNA breakage and cell death.

questions.rationale: Topoisomerase inhibitors disrupt the actions needed to maintain DNA during copying, causing DNA breakage and cell death.

questions.stem: Which serious adverse effect is associated in Appendix D with mitotic inhibitors such as vincristine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Peripheral nerve damage that may be permanent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excessive estrogen production.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Severe hypoglycemia from increased insulin release.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of aldosterone with hyperkalemia.

questions.rationale: The slides describe mitotic inhibitors as stopping cell division and note that peripheral nerve damage may be permanent.

questions.stem: Before an IV chemotherapy infusion, which access finding is important to verify?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The IV has no blood return so the drug cannot move too quickly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The site is covered so it cannot be observed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The IV is in a large vein with good blood return.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The catheter is disconnected until the patient reports discomfort.

questions.rationale: Appendix D lists a large vein with good blood return and catheter checks as pre-infusion safety steps.

questions.stem: During the first part of an IV chemotherapy infusion, what observation does Appendix D specify?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leave the patient alone for 30 minutes if baseline vital signs are normal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes and check for allergic reactions every 15 minutes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Check the site only after the infusion is complete.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Assess for allergy once at the end of the treatment.

questions.rationale: Appendix D directs the nurse to remain with the patient for the first 15 minutes and monitor every 15 minutes for allergic reactions.

questions.stem: How often should the site of an infusing vesicant be assessed to help prevent extravasation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Once at the start of the infusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only if the patient reports pain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At the end of each treatment day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At least every 30 minutes.

questions.rationale: The slides specify assessment of vesicant flow and access site at least every 30 minutes to detect leakage early.

questions.stem: A patient develops signs of an acute reaction during chemotherapy. What is the first infusion-related action described in Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stop the infusion while preserving IV access for assessment and prescribed support treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flush the remaining chemotherapy rapidly into the patient.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Remove the IV immediately before assessing the patient.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wait until the next vital-sign check to decide whether to stop.

questions.rationale: For a suspected anaphylactic or adverse reaction, the slides say to prevent more drug from entering by stopping the infusion while keeping IV access available.

questions.stem: Who should use protective equipment when handling chemotherapy waste or patient excretions after IV chemotherapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only the oncology prescriber during the infusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only the patient, and only while in the infusion chair.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Workers handling the drugs, waste, or excretions within 48 hours after treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No one if the chemotherapy has already been disconnected.

questions.rationale: Appendix D calls for PPE when preparing, administering, disposing of chemotherapy, or handling waste/excretions within 48 hours after IV treatment.

questions.stem: A breast tumor depends on estrogen for growth. How does the aromatase inhibitor anastrozole help, according to Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases estrogen to protect the endometrium.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reduces estrogen production and lowers circulating estrogen, slowing growth of estrogen-sensitive cancer cells.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It directly cross-links tumor DNA as an alkylating agent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It blocks insulin receptors in the tumor.

questions.rationale: The slides state that anastrozole prevents estrogen production in the adrenal gland, reducing blood estrogen and slowing estrogen-sensitive breast cancer growth.

questions.stem: Which adverse effect pattern is associated with aromatase inhibitors in Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Severe hypoglycemia and injection-site lipodystrophy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peripheral edema with acute hearing loss only.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutropenia without any other possible effect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bone, muscle, or joint pain and increased osteoporosis risk.

questions.rationale: Appendix D lists bone, muscle, and joint pain with aromatase inhibitors and notes osteoporosis risk.

questions.stem: Why may a patient with prostate cancer receive hormone-manipulation therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Androgen signaling can increase growth of some prostate cancer cells, so therapy suppresses androgen production or function.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Progesterone directly stimulates prostate-cell growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Estrogen is required to make prostate cancer cells metastasize.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hormone therapy is used to make chemotherapy local rather than systemic.

questions.rationale: The slides explain that testosterone binding to androgen receptors can increase prostate cancer growth; therapy suppresses androgen production or function.

questions.stem: Which effect should be included when teaching about prostate-cancer hormone therapy described in Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The medication guarantees the cancer is cured.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The therapy commonly causes immediate hair regrowth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hot flashes, reduced libido, or sexual dysfunction may occur.

choices.label: D
choices.text: There are no possible effects on fluid balance or liver enzymes.

questions.rationale: Appendix D lists gynecomastia, reduced libido or sexual dysfunction, hot flashes, fluid retention, fatigue, and other possible effects.

questions.stem: How can progestin therapy help treat endometrial cancer, according to Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It increases estrogen exposure to stimulate endometrial growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continuous progestin exposure can thin the uterine lining and cause endometrial-cell atrophy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It blocks DNA topoisomerase in all rapidly dividing cells.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It causes androgen receptors to bind more strongly.

questions.rationale: The slides explain that progesterone/progestins inhibit endometrial-cell growth; continuous treatment can thin the lining and cause cell atrophy.

questions.stem: What must be true for a targeted biologic therapy to work against a particular cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cancer must be benign and remain encapsulated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The patient must have received radiation first in every case.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug must target a feature found only in all normal cells.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cancer cells must have enough of the specific target the drug is designed to affect.

questions.rationale: Appendix D notes that the cancer must express sufficient amounts of the specific target; not all cancers of the same type have the same target.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how targeted therapy differs from traditional chemotherapy in Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It focuses on specific cancer-cell features and may spare many normal cells that are rapidly dividing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It affects only the original tumor and cannot reach distant sites.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is guaranteed to cure cancer after one treatment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It works only by causing hair follicles to stop dividing.

questions.rationale: The slides contrast traditional chemotherapy, which affects rapidly dividing normal and cancer cells, with targeted therapy, which focuses on specific cancer-cell features. Targeted therapy still has important risks and is not described as a guaranteed cure.

questions.stem: Which targeted therapy type is described as a lab-made protein that attaches to a specific target on the outside of a cancer cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alkylating agent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antimetabolite.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topoisomerase inhibitor.

questions.rationale: Appendix D describes monoclonal antibodies as lab-made proteins that attach to specific targets on the outside of cells; antibody therapies can cause allergic reactions.

questions.stem: What do tyrosine kinase inhibitors do, according to Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase estrogen production to stimulate tumor growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibit an enzyme involved in cancer-cell growth signaling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cross-link DNA strands like alkylating agents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cause all tumor cells to become encapsulated.

questions.rationale: Tyrosine kinases activate proteins in growth pathways. Inhibiting the enzyme can reduce growth signaling and slow or stop cancer-cell growth.

questions.stem: Which adverse-effect pattern is listed for multikinase inhibitors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only injection-site irritation with no systemic effects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Severe hypoglycemia as the expected class effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low potassium and slow heart rate in every patient.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypertension, nausea or vomiting, GI effects, and mild bone marrow suppression.

questions.rationale: Appendix D lists hypertension, nausea/vomiting, other GI disturbances, and mild bone marrow suppression among common multikinase inhibitor effects.

questions.stem: Which adverse effects are listed for proteasome inhibitors in Appendix D?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nausea or vomiting, anorexia, GI effects, and peripheral neuropathy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess estrogen and increased uterine lining growth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only mild hair thinning without other effects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypercalcemia and kidney stones as the defining pattern.

questions.rationale: The slides list nausea/vomiting, anorexia, GI effects, and peripheral neuropathy as possible effects of proteasome inhibitors.

questions.stem: How does Appendix D characterize the goal of biologic targeted cancer therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cures every cancer that expresses a target.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It replaces all other cancer treatment and removes the need for monitoring.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It can provide temporary disease control and prolong time before progression, but is not presented as a cure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents cancer cells from ever developing resistance.

questions.rationale: Appendix D describes targeted biologic therapy as temporary control that may delay progression and debilitation; it does not claim a cure, and effectiveness depends on the cancer having the target.
